doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Late Coltrane, Pharaoh Sanders and Alvin Thomas playing through illness
summary: Jordan on Trane's late playing and the Olatunji Center date, then Alvin Thomas playing on despite cancer; Rowe adds Lionel Hampton.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah you know, that’s right, what’s going on. Like you say Trane stark raving mad. Trane was just into his thing, I mean that’s what he wanted to do.
Where did that inspiration for that kind of playing come from? Do you have any idea?

I haven’t the slightest idea, well Trane heard everything. And he heard that the saxophone, like you heard that tune that he did at the Olatunji Center with he and Pharaoh Sanders, that live date that they did at Olatunji Center? I mean that was a hell of a date. I mean they were completely out on that. But Trane was playing on some of the things that he heard the way he put them scales together. I got a good idea how he put all that together. And I talked to Pharaoh about that and he said, “man look, that was just a few Hallelujahs.”

Hallelujah. I mean Trane, you know, and when you get to that point, and I think he was sick because that might have been one of the last recordings. So I mean they just pulled everything out. And I wish I could have been there just to hear it in person, just hearing it the way it is is really, they’re really on top of it.
Just physically to pull that off.

That’s right. And him being ill man. I mean that was a hell of a feat. That’s right. But you know what? Now Clyde told you about a saxophone player named Alvin Thomas. We played a gig with Alvin Thomas and we didn’t know he had cancer. And he told me, he said, man I was up at the thing and he was playing so much at a jazz festival and he said he was going over. And he said it looked like somebody, Trane or somebody, hit him on the back and says, “stand up there.” And he stood up and played like there was no tomorrow. And when he came down off the stand we had to stop with him in the car before we got home because the cancer, even though we didn’t know he was that ill. So that’s some forces that can keep somebody, when you get the energy. I don’t know where it comes from but it can keep you going for a minute at least.
I mean he’d shuffle out on stage and it would take him five minutes to get across the stage and then you couldn’t stop him.
